qs.q:
UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM — NGỮ PHÁP & TỪ VỰNG (ĐỀ 1): Mark the letter A, B, C, or D on your answer sheet to indicate the correct answer to each of the following questions.
U Minh Thượng ______ Park in Kiên Giang Province is famous for its tropical peat-swamp forest and rare waterbirds.
qs.ex: Ngữ pháp Unit 10 (Compound nouns): National Park = Vườn quốc gia.

qs.q: When one predator disappears, the entire marine ______ chain can collapse.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép (Compound noun) Unit 10: food chain = chuỗi thức ăn.

qs.q: Tropical ______ cover only a small part of the Earth’s surface, yet they are home to over half of the world’s flora and fauna.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép Unit 10: rainforests = rừng mưa nhiệt đới.

qs.q: Planting ______ tree species helps restore degraded forest ecosystems much better than importing foreign trees.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: native species = các loài bản địa.

qs.q: Burning coal and oil releases carbon dioxide, which intensifies the ______ effect and warms the planet.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép Unit 10: greenhouse effect = hiệu ứng nhà kính.

qs.q: The rich ______ and fauna of Cúc Phương National Park attract thousands of nature lovers and researchers every year.
qs.ex: Cụm từ cố định Unit 10: flora and fauna = hệ thực vật và động vật.

qs.q: During autumn, the coastal mangrove forest becomes a safe stopover for thousands of migratory ______.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép Unit 10: waterbirds = chim nước.

qs.q: Releasing pet red-eared sliders into local ponds is dangerous because they are an ______ species that outcompetes native turtles.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: invasive species = loài ngoại lai xâm hại.

qs.q: Many tourists visit the coral reef in summer to go ______ and admire colourful tropical fish.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: go snorkelling / scuba diving = lặn ngắm san hô.

qs.q: Climate ______ is causing more frequent droughts and forest fires across Southeast Asia.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép Unit 10: climate change = biến đổi khí hậu.

qs.q: Tiny bacteria and fungi play a vital role in the ecosystem by breaking down dead ______ matter into soil nutrients.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: organic matter = chất hữu cơ.

qs.q: Overuse of chemical pesticides on farms destroys beneficial insects and pollutes underground ______ supplies.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép: water supplies = nguồn cung cấp nước.

qs.q: Strict laws have been passed to ban illegal ______ of rare orchids and timber in the nature reserve.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: illegal logging = khai thác gỗ trái phép.

qs.q: A healthy ______ consists of all the living organisms in an area interacting with non-living elements like air, water and soil.
qs.ex: Từ vựng Unit 10: ecosystem = hệ sinh thái.

qs.q: Early morning is the best time for ______ in the wetland reserve because hundreds of storks gather to feed.
qs.ex: Danh từ ghép (Noun + V-ing) Unit 10: bird-watching = ngắm chim.

Educators and families also note that **(3)**______ prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds. qs.q:
Mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best arrangement of utterances or sentences to make a cohesive and coherent exchange or text in each of the following questions from 7 to 11.
**Dear Alex,**
a. At school, our teachers also organise practical projects to help us protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance.
b. Thank you for your email; it was great to hear about your recent school activities.
c. At weekends, my friends and I join community groups to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands.
d. I’m writing to tell you about how we are learning about conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains in Unit 10: The Ecosystem.
e. Write back soon and tell me what your school is doing on this topic!
**Best wishes,**
qs.ex: Trình tự bức thư: Cảm ơn thư trước (b) → Nêu lý do viết thư chia sẻ chủ đề Unit (d) → Kể hoạt động ở trường (a) → Kể hoạt động cuối tuần (c) → Lời kết thư (e): b - d - a - c - e.

qs.q:
a. Nam: Yes, definitely! Let’s sign up together after class today.
b. Mai: Nam, our school club is holding a workshop on conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains this Saturday. Would you like to join?
c. Mai: Great! I’ll get two registration forms from the club leader.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 3 lượt: Mai rủ Nam tham gia workshop chủ đề Unit (b) → Nam đồng ý đăng ký (a) → Mai nói sẽ đi lấy phiếu đăng ký (c): b - a - c.

qs.q:
a. To address this, schools and communities are now launching new natural ecosystems in national parks and wetlands.
b. In the past, many people did not pay enough attention to conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains.
c. Today, however, both biologists, rangers and students realise how important it is to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats.
d. As a result, everyone benefits when we work together to prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
e. These practical programmes help participants protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance in their daily lives.
qs.ex: Trình tự đoạn văn 5 câu: Thực trạng trước đây (b) → Nhận thức thay đổi ngày nay (c) → Giải pháp triển khai chương trình mới (a) → Tác dụng của các chương trình đó ('These practical programmes') (e) → Kết quả chung (d): b - c - a - e - d.

qs.q:
a. Linh: I’m preparing a poster about conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains for our English lesson tomorrow.
b. Minh: That sounds interesting! What main benefit are you highlighting on the poster?
c. Minh: Well done, Linh. I’m sure our classmates will learn a lot from your presentation!
d. Linh: I’m focusing on how natural ecosystems can protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance and prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
e. Minh: What are you working on, Linh? You look really focused.
qs.ex: Trình tự hội thoại 5 lượt: Minh hỏi Linh đang làm gì (e) → Linh nói đang làm poster cho bài học tiếng Anh (a) → Minh hỏi lợi ích chính trên poster là gì (b) → Linh giải thích nội dung (d) → Minh khen ngợi (c): e - a - b - d - c.

qs.q:
a. Next, participants work in small groups to discuss practical ways to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats.
b. After the opening talk, the organisers show a short video on how natural ecosystems work in national parks and wetlands.

**PERSPECTIVES ON THE ECOSYSTEM**
In recent years, conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains has attracted growing attention from educators and researchers alike. A recent national survey reports that while over eighty per cent of biologists, rangers and students recognise the importance of natural ecosystems, only about thirty-five per cent have <u>**restored**</u> these practices into their daily routines in national parks and wetlands. Even when resources are available, many people still struggle to balance their busy schedules with the need to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats.
The challenge lies not only in awareness but also in daily habits. Researchers note that active participants regularly engage in structured tasks that protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance, whereas passive observers only join occasional events once or twice a year. Consistent practice requires patience and planning, but it delivers lasting rewards. Many individuals simply repeat outdated habits they observed in the past, which prevents them from experiencing how natural ecosystems can prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
Fortunately, attitudes are shifting rapidly. **[I]** Most respondents in the survey agreed that everyone should conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats, even though many admitted spending less than two hours a week on it themselves. **[II]** Progress was strongest in communities where schools and families worked together as partners. **[III]** Groups can begin by setting clear weekly goals and giving every member a practical role in national parks and wetlands. **[IV]** Small, steady steps like these can turn a difficult challenge into a shared habit of cooperation.
Promoting conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains matters for the long-term future. Young people who see biologists, rangers and students model positive behaviours are likely to view these practices as normal, and <u>**they**</u> will carry those values into adulthood. In this way, natural ecosystems not only protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance today but also prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds for generations to come.
(Adapted from Educational & Social Research Reports – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

**MAKING THE ECOSYSTEM PART OF DAILY LIFE**
Taking time to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats may seem ordinary at first glance, yet a growing body of research highlights its transformative power. Studies show that well-designed natural ecosystems help biologists, rangers and students protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance. At the same time, these practices prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds and foster stronger cooperation in national parks and wetlands.
Despite these clear advantages, participation in natural ecosystems has faced obstacles in recent years. Researchers report that <u>**they**</u> have been neglected in many busy communities due to modern time pressures. <u>**Tight timetables, heavy workloads and a lack of practical guidance can all prevent people from maintaining positive routines.**</u> Even when individuals want to improve, distractions often get in the way.
The encouraging news is that success does not require perfection from day one. Experts emphasise that building <u>**native**</u> habits is about steady progress rather than instant results. Biologists, rangers and students can start with simple steps in national parks and wetlands, share responsibilities and use practical checklists to stay on track. Those who understand the purpose behind conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains become much more resilient and motivated.
Of course, no single workshop or rule will solve every challenge overnight, and some groups need time to adapt. That is no reason to give up. Even one or two focused sessions a week can spark meaningful change, and the positive <u>**species**</u> will grow stronger over time. What matters most is the commitment people bring to supporting one another every day.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**PARTNERSHIPS BETWEEN SCHOOLS AND FAMILIES IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
Over the past two years, a research team from the National Institute of Education has tracked 1,500 high school students to evaluate how conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains affects teenager development. The study found that while nearly ninety per cent of biologists, rangers and students valued natural ecosystems, only forty-two per cent <u>**sustained**</u> these routines throughout the entire school year. Students who tried to practise alone often gave up after a few weeks when exam pressure increased.
By contrast, learners whose families and teachers coordinated their guidance achieved far more durable results. In households where parents actively joined weekend activities to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands, teenagers were twice as likely to protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance. Researchers explained that shared routines reduce the feeling of isolation and turn abstract classroom advice into enjoyable daily habits. Moreover, consistent family involvement helps prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds without adding extra stress to students’ timetables.
Schools across the country are now redesigning their programmes based on these findings. **[I]** Instead of assigning theoretical worksheets, teachers invite parents and students to co-sign a simple weekly action plan. **[II]** This joint commitment ensures that classroom lessons are reinforced at home every evening. **[III]** At monthly review sessions, classes celebrate collective progress and exchange practical solutions to common obstacles. **[IV]**
The long-term implications of this partnership model are encouraging. When biologists, rangers and students work side by side, <u>**they**</u> build mutual respect and lasting life skills. Ultimately, integrating conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains into both school curricula and family life prepares young citizens to thrive in an increasingly complex world.
(Adapted from National Educational Research Reports – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

qs.ex: sustained = maintained (duy trì bền bỉ suốt cả năm học).

**WHY CONSISTENCY MATTERS MORE THAN PERFECTION IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
When people first decide to focus on conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains, they often set overly ambitious targets. Enthusiastic beginners might promise to transform their entire lifestyle in a single weekend, only to feel exhausted a few days later. Studies on habit formation show that well-paced natural ecosystems are far more effective when built step by step, helping biologists, rangers and students protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance without burnout.
The main reason crash campaigns fail is that <u>**they**</u> demand too much willpower at once. <u>**Small, consistent efforts practised every day produce far more lasting results than occasional bursts of intense activity.**</u> When a routine fits naturally into a family’s or student’s daily schedule, it requires less mental strain to maintain.
Experts therefore recommend a <u>**gradual**</u> approach to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands. By starting with one simple task each day and celebrating weekly milestones, learners steadily build momentum. Such steady practice not only strengthens personal discipline but also helps communities prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
Of course, occasional setbacks are normal during busy exam weeks or family events. Rather than abandoning the goal altogether, resilient learners simply resume their routine the next morning, knowing that patience will <u>**foster**</u> long-term success.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**COMMUNITY ACTION AND PEER MENTORING IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
Last year, youth unions in three provinces launched a six-month pilot programme to promote conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains at the grassroots level. Instead of relying on formal lectures, organisers trained two hundred high school volunteers to lead weekend activities where neighbours could conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands. Within the first two months, local communities reported <u>**tangible**</u> improvements in daily habits and neighbourhood solidarity.
A key factor behind this success was peer-to-peer mentoring. Teenagers often feel intimidated when adults lecture them, but they respond enthusiastically when classmates demonstrate how natural ecosystems can protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance. By working in small teams of five or six, participants shared practical tips, solved everyday problems together and helped one another prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
Organisers also introduced simple tools to keep momentum high. **[I]** Every participating household received a visual progress board to track weekly milestones. **[II]** Local cultural centres hosted monthly gatherings where teams showcased their most creative ideas. **[III]** These celebrations turned routine tasks into a source of shared pride across the entire district. **[IV]**
Follow-up surveys conducted six months later confirmed that over seventy-five per cent of participants continued practising natural ecosystems independently. When student volunteers take ownership of community initiatives, <u>**their**</u> enthusiasm inspires both younger children and older residents. The pilot programme demonstrates that youth-led action is one of the most powerful ways to bring the values of Unit 10: The Ecosystem to life.
(Adapted from Community Development & Youth Studies – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

qs.ex: tangible = rõ rệt, hữu hình, có thể nhận thấy thực tế (noticeable and real).

**THE RIPPLE EFFECT OF PEER LEADERSHIP IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
How do positive habits spread across a school or neighbourhood? Sociologists studying conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains have discovered that peer influence is often stronger than formal rules. When biologists, rangers and students see their close friends willingly engage in natural ecosystems, they are far more likely to join in and protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance.
Nevertheless, launching a new initiative is never without challenges. Organisers note that initial doubts and busy routines are common, and <u>**they**</u> can slow down participation during the first week. <u>**Young people learn most effectively when they observe respected peers applying positive habits in real-life situations.**</u>
For this reason, many schools encourage <u>**voluntary**</u> student ambassadors to lead by example. Whether demonstrating how to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands or sharing practical tips during break time, these role models create a welcoming ripple effect that helps the whole school prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds.
Even when a minor <u>**obstacle**</u> arises, a supportive peer group keeps members motivated. What begins as the effort of a few enthusiastic students soon grows into a proud tradition shared by the entire community.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

**Read the passage and mark the letter A, B, C or D on your answer sheet to indicate the best answer to each of the following questions from 17 to 26.**

**OVERCOMING BARRIERS TO DAILY PRACTICE IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
Why do many high school students agree that conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains is important, yet still find it difficult to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands every day? Educational psychologists point out that modern teenagers face three main barriers: digital distractions, academic pressure and a lack of structured routines. When students feel overwhelmed, they often become <u>**reluctant**</u> to take on new responsibilities at home or in the community.
Fortunately, behavioural research shows that breaking large goals into micro-habits can overcome this hesitation. Instead of trying to change everything overnight, biologists, rangers and students can start with a fifteen-minute daily routine focused on natural ecosystems. These manageable actions quickly build confidence and help learners protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance without interfering with their homework.
Another effective strategy is using a structured weekly checklist. **[I]** When teenagers write down specific times and places for their tasks, they are three times more likely to follow through. **[II]** Sharing <u>**it**</u> with a supportive classmate or family member adds friendly accountability. **[III]** Rather than feeling pressured, students enjoy tracking their streak of completed tasks and seeing how their efforts prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds. **[IV]**
Teachers who have introduced micro-habits and checklists into their lessons on Unit 10: The Ecosystem report remarkable improvements in student engagement. Once young people realise that small daily choices lead to meaningful results, natural ecosystems stops feeling like a burden and becomes a natural part of who they are.
(Adapted from Adolescent Psychology & Education Review – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)
qs.q: The word **<u>reluctant</u>** in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ______.
qs.ex: reluctant = ngần ngại, miễn cưỡng (hesitant and unwilling).

**EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND THE FUTURE OF UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
Across Viet Nam, forward-thinking high schools are transforming how students learn about conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains. Rather than treating Unit 10: The Ecosystem as a set of vocabulary items to memorise for a test, teachers are integrating experiential learning into every week of the semester. Educators agree that hands-on practice is <u>**indispensable**</u> if young people are to protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance.
In these classrooms, students work in project teams to investigate real issues and propose ways to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands. For instance, learners might interview local residents, design bilingual awareness posters or organise a school-wide campaign on natural ecosystems. Through these authentic tasks, biologists, rangers and students discover how their classroom English connects directly to everyday life.
Assessment methods are evolving alongside teaching styles. **[I]** Instead of relying solely on written quizzes, schools evaluate how effectively students collaborate and apply their plans. **[II]** Each team keeps a reflective portfolio documenting the challenges they faced and how their actions helped prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds. **[III]** This approach rewards creativity, persistence and genuine teamwork rather than rote memorisation. **[IV]**
Graduates of experiential programmes consistently report higher confidence when entering university and the workplace. Students <u>**who**</u> have practised solving real-world problems in high school adapt much faster to new environments. By making conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains an active, lived experience, education equips the next generation with both language proficiency and civic responsibility.
(Adapted from Modern Curriculum & Pedagogy Journal – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

**SELF-REFLECTION AND LONG-TERM GROWTH IN UNIT 10: THE ECOSYSTEM**
Practising natural ecosystems is even more rewarding when learners take a few minutes each week to reflect on their progress. Educators studying conserving native flora and fauna, wetlands and food chains have found that students who keep a brief weekly journal understand their own habits much better and find it easier to protect native flora and fauna and keep food chains in balance.
During busy weeks, people sometimes miss a planned task or make mistakes. Without reflection, <u>**they**</u> may feel discouraged and assume that their efforts have failed. <u>**Honest self-reflection allows learners to turn early mistakes into valuable lessons rather than reasons to give up.**</u>
To make reflection effective, teachers recommend asking <u>**constructive**</u> questions every Sunday evening: What went well when we tried to conserve biodiversity and restore degraded habitats in national parks and wetlands this week, and what small adjustment will help us improve next week?
Over time, this simple habit deepens personal <u>**commitment**</u> and helps biologists, rangers and students prevent soil erosion, store carbon and shelter migratory birds with confidence and pride.
(Adapted from Global Success Reading Series – Unit 10: The Ecosystem)

It requires learners to write fifty pages every night.
